concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.hook: Five ₹20 idlis fit a ₹100 note; after each idli becomes ₹25, only four fit. The note has not changed. What did?
concepts.rule: Inflation is the yearly rise in prices across a basket of everyday goods. When prices rise faster than your money, it buys less. India's central bank aims for about 4%.

claims.text: India uses a consumer price index to track change in a basket of retail prices.
A rise in broad prices cuts the buying power of cash if its amount stays fixed.
India's inflation rate compares prices in one month with the same month a year earlier. Survey staff record prices in markets across India every month.
If income rises less than prices, real income falls; people on fixed incomes lose buying power.
India's inflation target is 4%, with a low limit of 2% and a top limit of 6%, set until March 2031. Falling prices can make people put off buying.

items.stem: Your hostel rent rises 8% this year, and your stipend also rises 8%. What happens to what the stipend covers?

options.text: It covers about the same as before.
options.feedback: Both grew at the same speed, so you are neither ahead nor behind on rent.

options.text: It covers more, because the stipend went up.
options.feedback: A raise only helps if it beats the price rise. Here they match, so nothing changes.

options.text: It covers less, because rent went up.
options.feedback: Rent rose, but the stipend rose just as fast, so the same share of rent is covered.

items.stem: Prices rise at the RBI's target rate for years. Your ₹20,000 savings account pays 3% a year. What happens to what it buys?

options.text: It buys a little less each year.
options.feedback: Yes. The target is about 4%, more than the 3% you earn, so prices outrun your savings.

options.text: It buys a little more each year, since interest keeps adding rupees.
options.feedback: The rupees grow, but only 3%. Prices rise about 4%, so each year the money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, because the target keeps prices still.
options.feedback: The target is not zero. It aims for prices to rise about 4% a year, not to stay still.

items.stem: The same basket costs ₹1,080 this May, after 8% inflation. About what did it cost last May?

options.feedback: Yes. Last year times 1.08 gives ₹1,080, so divide 1,080 by 1.08 to get ₹1,000.

options.text: About ₹994, which is 8% off this year's price.
options.feedback: Taking 8% off the new price uses the wrong base. The 8% was added to last year's price, so divide by 1.08.
That adds another 8% on top. Going back a year means removing the rise, so divide by 1.08.

items.stem: Tomatoes went from ₹40 to ₹60 a kilo this year. A friend says inflation must be 50%. What is the flaw?

options.text: Tomatoes are one item, and most other prices moved far less.
options.feedback: Right. Inflation is the rise across the whole basket, so one jump moves it only a little.

options.text: The rise is ₹20, so inflation is 20%.
options.feedback: The rupee gap is not a percent, and one item still is not the whole basket of prices.

options.text: It is right; one big price rise sets the rate.
options.feedback: One item is a small part of a very big basket, so it cannot set the overall rate.

items.stem: Your pay rose 4% this year, yet it buys less than last year. What must be true about prices?

options.feedback: Pay that buys less after a raise means prices grew faster than the raise did.

options.text: They rose by less than 4%, which made your raise shrink.
options.feedback: If prices rose less than your pay, your pay would buy more, not less.
Falling prices would make the same pay buy more. Buying less points to prices rising faster.

items.stem: A 2% raise while prices climb 9% leaves you behind, because the raise ___.

options.text: is smaller than the rise in prices
options.feedback: Yes. Your rupees grew 2% but prices grew 9%, so your pay now buys less.

options.text: still adds more rupees to every pay slip you get
options.feedback: More rupees is true, but they buy less when prices grow faster than pay.
How often the raise comes is not the issue. Its size against prices is what counts.

items.stem: A friend says any inflation at all means the economy is in trouble. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Mild, steady rises are normal, since falling prices make people put off buying.
options.feedback: Right. A little inflation keeps people buying, which is why the RBI aims above zero.

options.text: He is right; the safest goal is zero inflation.
options.feedback: Zero is not the goal. Falling or flat prices can make people wait to buy, which slows things.

options.text: Inflation is harmless at any level.
options.feedback: Fast inflation does hurt buying power. The point is that a little is normal, not that any amount is fine.

items.stem: Put these in order to find how much your hostel mess bill rose in a year, in percent.

options.text: Find this month's bill and the bill for the same month last year.
options.feedback: You compare the same month a year apart, just as the inflation figure does.

options.text: Subtract to get the rise in rupees.
options.feedback: The gap between the two bills shows how many rupees more you pay now.

options.text: Divide the rise by last year's bill, then multiply by 100.
options.feedback: Dividing by the older bill turns the rupee rise into a yearly percent rise.

misconceptions.name: One price is the index
misconceptions.correction: One snack can rise while the broad basket moves in a different way.

misconceptions.name: Same cash, same goods
misconceptions.correction: When broad prices rise, the same cash can buy fewer goods.

misconceptions.name: Any raise makes you better off
misconceptions.correction: A raise smaller than the rise in prices still buys less than before.

misconceptions.name: The goal is zero inflation
misconceptions.correction: A little inflation is normal, since falling prices make people wait to buy. India's target is about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

steps.title: Inflation is prices rising across a basket

hook.stem: Say the news reports a 3% price rise (inflation) for May. What does that mean?

options.text: Everyday prices are about 3% above last May.
options.feedback: Right. It compares a big basket of everyday prices with the same month a year before.
Some prices jump and some barely move. The 3% is the overall change across the basket.
The figure compares this May with last May, a full year apart, not with the month before.

steps.teach: Inflation is how much prices rose in a year. India tracks a big basket of everyday goods, because one item, like onions, can jump while others stay flat. Each month is compared with the same month last year.

example.ask: Tap the comparison.
parts: Rice, milk and bus fares in the big list
cost 3% more than they did last May,
so the news reports 3% inflation.
example.spot: cost 3% more than they did last May,
example.feedback: Inflation compares the same basket with the same month a year earlier.

guided.stem: Onions double in price, but most other prices barely move. What happens to inflation?
guided.hint: Onions are one item in a very big basket.

options.feedback: Yes. One item doubling moves the whole basket only a little when the rest stays flat.
Onions are a small part of the basket, so the overall rise is far smaller than double.
A price went up and the others held still, so the basket costs a bit more, not less.

guided.stem: This June's inflation figure is out. Which prices does it compare?
guided.hint: Seasons change prices, so match like with like.

options.feedback: Right. Matching the same month a year apart is how the rate is worked out.
A one-month gap is not used here. The rate compares the same month a year earlier.

options.text: This June against ten years ago.
options.feedback: Ten years is far too long a gap. The yearly rate compares with the same month last year.

steps.takeaway: Inflation is the yearly rise across a whole basket of prices.

steps.title: When prices outrun your money, it buys less

hook.stem: Your pocket money stays at ₹2,000 while prices rise 10%. What happens?

options.text: It buys about a tenth less.
options.feedback: Right. The note is the same, but each thing costs more, so the same money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, since it is still ₹2,000.
options.feedback: The number on the money stays put, but prices moved up, so it now covers less shopping.
Higher prices work the other way. The same ₹2,000 now covers less, not more.

steps.teach: When prices rise, each rupee buys less, so the same money covers less shopping. If your income grows slower than prices, you can buy less than last year, even with a raise.

example.ask: Tap why she is behind.
parts: Kavya got a 5% raise this year,
but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
so her pay now buys less than before.
example.spot: but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
example.feedback: Her costs grew faster than her pay, so the raise did not keep up.

guided.stem: A ₹100 basket of shopping now costs ₹125. How much of it does ₹100 buy?
guided.hint: Work out 100 divided by 125.

options.feedback: Yes. 100 divided by 125 is 0.8, so the same cash covers 80% of the basket.
The basket now costs ₹125, more than you hold, so ₹100 cannot cover all of it.
That flips the sum. ₹125 is the new price, so ₹100 buys less than one basket.

guided.stem: Prices rise 5% this year. Whose pay keeps up?
guided.hint: Compare each pay rise with the 5% price rise.

options.feedback: Right. His pay grew faster than prices, so it buys a little more than last year.
Her pay rose, but slower than prices, so it buys less than it did last year.
With no rise at all, his same pay meets higher prices and buys less.

steps.takeaway: If prices grow faster than your money, you fall behind.

steps.title: A little inflation is normal, and the RBI aims for about 4%

hook.stem: What inflation rate do you think India's central bank aims for?

options.feedback: Right. The RBI's target is 4%, with a band from 2% to 6% around it.
The target is not zero. India aims for about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.
That would be far above the band. The upper limit is 6%, and the target is 4%.

steps.teach: A little inflation is normal. If prices fell every year, people would wait to buy and businesses would slow. So India's central bank aims for about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

example.ask: Tap why falling prices slow things.
parts: Prices drop a little every month,
so shoppers wait for an even lower price,
and shops sell less and hire fewer people.
example.spot: so shoppers wait for an even lower price,
example.feedback: When people expect lower prices later, they put off buying, and that slows the whole economy.

guided.stem: Prices in a country fall a little every year. What do many buyers do?
guided.hint: Think of a sale you know is coming next week.

options.text: Put off buying, hoping to pay less later.
options.feedback: Yes. If waiting makes things cheaper, many people wait, so shops sell less.
Buying now makes sense when prices will rise. When they fall, waiting pays, so people hold back.
Prices people expect do change behaviour. Falling prices give a reason to wait.

guided.stem: Inflation comes in at 7% this year. Where is that against the RBI's band?
guided.hint: Picture where the band starts and stops.

options.feedback: Right. 7% is higher than the 6% upper limit of the band.
The target is 4%. At 7%, inflation is above even the 6% upper limit.
The lower limit is 2%. A rate of 7% is well above the whole band.

steps.takeaway: A little inflation is normal; India aims for about 4%.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.hook: ₹1 lakh growing at an example rate of 7% for 30 years becomes about ₹7.6 lakh. The last ten years add more than the first twenty.
concepts.rule: Compounding means a gain can earn a later gain when it stays in the pot. A SIP adds money at set times, but that does not promise a set return.

claims.text: Compound growth includes growth on past gains as well as the starting amount.
A SIP is a way to add money at set times; market returns are not fixed, because investments can rise or fall in value.
Saved at 5% a year, 365 grows to about 466 after five years and about 1,578 after thirty years.
The sooner saving starts, the more time compound interest has to build it up.

items.stem: ₹4,000 grew to ₹4,840 in two years of compound interest, with gains left in. About what yearly rate did it earn?

options.feedback: Yes. ₹4,000 grows to ₹4,400 in year one, and 10% of ₹4,400 adds ₹440 to make ₹4,840.

options.text: About 10.5%, the ₹840 gain split over two years.
options.feedback: Splitting the gain evenly ignores growth on growth. Year two earned on the bigger pot, so the rate is 10%.
That is the whole two-year gain as one percent. Per year, with gains kept in, the rate is 10%.

items.stem: Tanvi says ₹3,000 at 10% a year for three years adds exactly ₹900 if gains stay in. What is she missing?

options.text: Each year, 10% works on a bigger sum.
options.feedback: Kept gains grow the base, so the years add ₹300, ₹330 and ₹363. That is ₹993, not ₹900.

options.text: The 10% counts in the first year, then stops.
options.feedback: The rate applies every year. Each year it works on the sum plus the gains kept in.

options.text: She is right; three years of 10% is ₹900.
options.feedback: That treats each year as earning on the first ₹3,000 only. Kept gains earn too, so it adds ₹993.

items.stem: Your ₹7,000 deposit pays 10% a year, and you take the interest out to spend each time. What happens to your yearly gain?

options.feedback: Right. With nothing left in, the pot never grows, so there is no gain on past gains.

options.text: It grows a little each year, as compound gains do.
options.feedback: Growth on growth needs the gain to stay in. Spent interest cannot earn anything more.
The pot stays at ₹7,000, so 10% of it stays ₹700. It neither grows nor shrinks.

items.stem: Riya puts ₹10,000 away at 21. Dev starts at 26 at the same rate and wants as much as Riya at 50. What must Dev do?

options.feedback: Yes. His money has five fewer years to grow, so he needs a bigger start to catch up.
The same sum with fewer years ends smaller, because it has less time to build on gains.

options.text: Put in less, since he starts later and saves on time.
options.feedback: Starting later gives less time to grow, not more. He needs a bigger sum, not a smaller one.

items.stem: A friend says starting to save at 25 instead of 22 costs nothing, since three years is small next to thirty. What is the flaw?

options.text: Fewer years means less growth on growth, so the end pot is smaller.
options.feedback: Right. Every year counts, because each one lets the gains build on a bigger pot.

options.text: He is right; the last few years matter most.
options.feedback: The last years add the most, but they can only do that on a pot built in the early years.

options.text: Rates are lower for people who start late.
options.feedback: The rate can be the same. The loss comes from having fewer years to grow.

items.stem: Which ends with more at 9% a year: ₹10,000 left for 24 years, or ₹20,000 left for 12 years?

options.feedback: It grows to about ₹79,100. The ₹20,000 grows to about ₹56,300, as it has half the time.
Starting bigger helps, but twelve extra years of growth on growth help more here.

options.text: They tie, as sum times years matches.
options.feedback: Growth is not sum times years. Each extra year multiplies the pot, so the longer one ends higher.

items.stem: A SIP can still lose money in a bad year, because ___.

options.text: the fund's investments can fall in price
options.feedback: Yes. A SIP sets the sum and the dates, but what the fund holds can still drop in value.

options.text: the payments stop when prices fall
options.feedback: Payments keep going on the set dates. The loss comes from the fund's value falling, not from missed payments.

options.text: a SIP pays a fixed rate like a bank deposit
options.feedback: A SIP has no fixed rate. Its value moves with what the fund holds, so it can fall.

items.stem: Two friends run ₹2,000 monthly SIPs in the same fund. One starts at 22, one at 30, and both stop at 50. What can you say?

options.text: The early starter will likely end with more, but neither result is promised.
options.feedback: Right. More years give more time to compound, yet the market still sets the actual growth.

options.text: Both end the same, since they pay the same each month.
options.feedback: The early starter pays for more years, and those years also have longer to grow.

options.text: The early starter is sure to end with twice as much.
options.feedback: No SIP result is sure. The market sets the growth, so no exact amount can be promised.

misconceptions.name: Gain only on start
misconceptions.correction: When gains stay in the pot, later gains can build on them too.

misconceptions.name: SIP means sure gain
misconceptions.correction: A SIP sets a payment pattern; it does not set market returns.

misconceptions.name: A late start costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: Starting later gives money fewer years to grow, so it ends smaller.

steps.title: Gains start earning gains

hook.stem: Sana and Om each save ₹1,000 at 10%. Sana leaves her interest in; Om spends his. Who has more after two years?

options.feedback: Right. Her ₹100 gain stayed in and earned ₹10 more in year two.
Om has ₹1,000 plus ₹200 spent. Sana's kept gain earned extra, so she has ₹1,210.
Spending the interest means it cannot earn more. Sana ends with ₹1,210 saved.

steps.teach: With compound interest, you earn on your savings and on the interest they already made. So each year's gain is a bit bigger.

example.ask: Tap the interest on interest.
parts: Meera's ₹1,000 earned ₹100 in year one.
In year two, that ₹100 earned ₹10 of its own,
so her gain grew from ₹100 to ₹110.
example.spot: In year two, that ₹100 earned ₹10 of its own,
example.feedback: The ₹10 came from last year's gain, not from her first ₹1,000.

guided.stem: ₹500 earns 10% a year and the gain stays in. What is it worth after one year?
guided.hint: Find a tenth of the starting sum, then add it on.

options.feedback: Yes. 10% of ₹500 is ₹50, so the pot is now ₹550.
That adds only ₹10. 10% of ₹500 is ₹50, which makes ₹550.
That adds ₹100, which is 20%. At 10% the gain is ₹50.

guided.stem: In year two, the ₹550 earns 10% again. How big is the new gain?
guided.hint: Work out the rate on the new total, not on the first sum.

options.feedback: Right. The rate now works on ₹550, so the gain grows to ₹55.
That is 10% of the old ₹500. The pot is now ₹550, so the gain is ₹55.
That is only the gain on last year's gain. The full gain is 10% of ₹550, or ₹55.

steps.takeaway: Gains you leave in start to earn gains too.

steps.title: Time does most of the work

hook.stem: You save ₹365 once at 5% a year and leave it. About how much is it after 30 years?

options.feedback: Right. Growth on growth for 30 years takes ₹365 to about ₹1,578.
That counts 5% of ₹365 each year, as if gains never earned. Compounding gives about ₹1,578.
That is the value after five years. Twenty-five more years take it near ₹1,578.

steps.teach: Growth on growth is slow at first and fast later, because each year's gain is worked out on a bigger pot. Saved at 5%, ₹365 is about ₹466 after five years, but about ₹1,578 after thirty.

example.ask: Tap why Asha ends with more.
parts: Asha and Rohan both save at the same rate,
but Asha starts ten years sooner,
so her money has longer to grow.
example.spot: but Asha starts ten years sooner,
example.feedback: The same rate gives more when it has more years to work on past gains.

guided.stem: Kabir leaves ₹1,000 at 8% for 10 years. Ben leaves ₹1,000 at 8% for 20 years. How do they compare?
guided.hint: Ten more years of growth work on a bigger pot.

options.text: Ben has about twice as much.
options.feedback: Yes. Kabir reaches about ₹2,160; Ben reaches about ₹4,660.
That counts ₹80 a year with no growth on growth. Ben ends with about twice as much.
Ben's money grows for ten more years, so he ends with far more.

guided.stem: Over 30 years at 5%, which five years add the most rupees?
guided.hint: Ask when the pot is at its biggest.

options.feedback: Right. By then the pot is largest, so the same 5% adds the most rupees.
The pot is smallest then, so 5% adds the fewest rupees.

options.text: Every five-year span adds the same.
options.feedback: Each span starts from a bigger pot, so later spans add more.

steps.takeaway: The longer money grows, the faster it grows.

steps.title: A SIP is a habit, not a promise

hook.stem: A SIP takes ₹500 from your account every month. What does it fix?

options.text: How much goes in, and when.
options.feedback: Right. A SIP sets the sum and the dates. The market sets the return.
A SIP does not fix the return. The fund's value moves with the market.

options.text: That the fund keeps going up.
options.feedback: Funds can fall as well as rise. A SIP just keeps adding money on set dates.

steps.teach: A SIP (systematic investment plan) puts in the same sum at set times, like ₹500 each month. It gives money years to compound, but it cannot set the growth, because the fund's investments rise and fall in price.

example.ask: Tap the part a SIP cannot promise.
parts: Ravi sets up a ₹1,000 SIP each month,
the money goes in on the 5th,
and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.spot: and the fund's value moves with the market.
example.feedback: Ravi controls the sum and the date. The market decides how the fund's value moves.

guided.stem: A friend says a SIP fund is safe because money goes in every month. What is mixed up?
guided.hint: Ask what the regular part controls.

options.text: Paying often does not fix returns.
options.feedback: Yes. Regular payments set a habit. The fund can still fall.
A SIP takes money again and again. The mix-up is about returns.

options.text: The friend is right; monthly payments make it safe.
options.feedback: Monthly payments do not stop a fund from falling in a bad year.

guided.stem: Which of these does a ₹500 SIP set for you?
guided.hint: Think of what you choose when you sign up.

options.feedback: Right. You pick the sum and the dates when you start.
No one can set that. The market decides the return.
A SIP has no say over how high or low the fund goes.

steps.takeaway: A SIP fixes what you put in, not what you get back.

concepts.title: The rule of 72
concepts.hook: At an example rate of 9%, 72 ÷ 9 says eight years to double. Working it out exactly gives close to eight, but not exactly eight.
concepts.rule: For a steady percent rate, divide 72 by the rate to guess the years to double. It works for unpaid debt too. It is a rough shortcut, not a promise of market growth.

claims.text: The rule of 72 is a rough way to guess when a sum may double. Divide 72 by a set rate.
Market returns do not have a fixed rate, so the shortcut is only a what-if tool there.
At 4% a year, savings double in about 18 years, since 72 divided by 4 is 18.
The rule works for debt too: an unpaid card balance at 18% interest doubles in about four years. One large Indian card issuer charges up to 3.75% a month, or 45% a year.

items.stem: Prices rise at a steady 3% a year. By the shortcut, about how many years until prices double?

options.feedback: The shortcut works for any steady rate, prices too. 72 divided by 3 gives about 24 years.
The rate is not the time. Dividing 72 by 3 gives about 24 years for prices to double.
That multiplies 72 by 3. The rule divides 72 by the rate, which gives about 24.

items.stem: To double money in 3 years, the shortcut says you need a steady rate of about ___.

options.feedback: Working backwards, 72 divided by 3 years gives a rate of about 24% a year.

options.text: 3% a year, the same as the years
options.feedback: At 3% the shortcut gives about 24 years, not 3. The rate and the years swap places.
That multiplies 72 by 3. Dividing 72 by the years gives the rate: about 24%.

items.stem: Your ₹50,000 deposit pays a steady 7%. The shortcut gives about 10.3 years to double. What should you expect?

options.text: Roughly ten years; the shortcut is close, not exact.
options.feedback: Right. Worked out exactly it is about 10.2 years, near the guess but not the same.
The rule is a quick guess. The real time is close to it but not an exact date.

options.text: Far longer, since the shortcut is usually way off.
options.feedback: For steady rates like this the guess is close. Here the exact answer is about 10.2 years.

items.stem: You owe ₹8,000 on a card. Each month you pay all the interest, but none of the ₹8,000. What happens to the balance?

options.feedback: Yes. No interest is left unpaid, so nothing is added and the debt cannot double.

options.text: It still doubles on the usual timeline.
options.feedback: Debt doubles only when unpaid interest is added on. Here all of it is paid each month.

options.text: It falls a little every month.
options.feedback: Paying only interest keeps the debt level. To shrink it, part of the ₹8,000 must be paid too.

items.stem: You have ₹15,000 saved at 8% and owe ₹15,000 on a card at 45%. Which doubles first, and about when?

options.text: The debt, in under two years.
options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 45 is about 1.6, while the savings need 72 ÷ 8, about nine years.

options.text: The savings, in about nine years.
options.feedback: Nine years is right for the savings, but the debt doubles far sooner, in under two years.

options.text: Both in about the same time, since they start equal.
options.feedback: Starting sums match, but rates do not. A higher rate doubles much faster.

items.stem: An unpaid loan doubled in about 8 years. Using the doubling shortcut backwards, roughly what yearly rate was it charged?

options.feedback: Going backwards, 72 divided by 8 years gives a yearly rate of about 9%.
Eight is the number of years. Dividing 72 by 8 gives the rate, about 9%.
That multiplies 8 by 8. The shortcut divides 72 by the years, giving about 9%.

items.stem: In one line, when does the doubling shortcut work well?

options.text: When the rate stays the same each year.
options.feedback: The rule turns one steady rate into a rough doubling time, so a fixed rate suits it.

options.text: For share prices, because they grow the most.
options.feedback: Fast growth is not the test. Share returns change each year, so the rule is only a what-if there.

options.text: For any return, even a jumpy one.
options.feedback: A return that jumps around has no single rate to divide by.

items.stem: A fund went up 25%, down 8%, then up 16%. Can the shortcut give its doubling date?

options.text: No; the rate keeps changing, so it is only a what-if.
options.feedback: Right. The rule needs one steady rate, and this fund's return moved every year.

options.text: Yes; use its best year, 25%, for about three years.
options.feedback: One good year does not set the next. A jumpy return gives the rule no steady rate.

options.text: Yes; add the three returns and divide by them.
options.feedback: Adding returns does not make them steady. The rule only fits a rate that holds.

misconceptions.name: Exact clock
misconceptions.correction: The rule gives a rough guess, not an exact date.

misconceptions.correction: Market gains can vary; the shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.

steps.title: Divide 72 by the rate

hook.stem: Money grows at a steady 6% a year. About how long until it doubles?

options.feedback: Right. 72 divided by 6 is 12, so about 12 years at a steady 6%.
That uses the rate as the years. Divide 72 by 6 to get about 12.
72 is the number you divide, not the answer. 72 ÷ 6 gives about 12 years.

steps.teach: To guess how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 8%, 72 ÷ 8 is 9, so about nine years. It is a quick guess, so it is close but not exact.

example.ask: Tap the shortcut sum.
parts: Nisha's savings grow at a steady 4% a year.
She works out 72 ÷ 4 = 18,
so they double in about 18 years.
example.spot: She works out 72 ÷ 4 = 18,
example.feedback: Dividing 72 by the rate gives the rough number of years to double.

guided.stem: A deposit pays a steady 9%. Roughly how many years to double?
guided.hint: Share 72 out by the rate.

options.feedback: Yes. 72 ÷ 9 is 8, so about eight years.
Nine is the rate. Dividing 72 by 9 gives about 8 years.
That multiplies 9 by 9. The rule divides 72 by 9.

guided.stem: Which rate doubles money in about 6 years?
guided.hint: Test each choice against the shortcut.

options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 12 is 6.
At 6%, 72 ÷ 6 gives 12 years, not 6.
At 72%, money would double in about one year by the rule.

steps.takeaway: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate.

steps.title: Debt doubles the same way

hook.stem: A card balance of ₹10,000 is left unpaid at 36% a year. About when does it reach ₹20,000?

options.feedback: Right. 72 ÷ 36 is 2, so unpaid card debt at that rate doubles in about two years.
The rate is not the years. 72 divided by 36 gives about two.
Interest keeps adding to the unpaid balance, so it grows on its own.

steps.teach: The rule works on debt too, because unpaid interest is added to what you owe and then earns interest itself. Some Indian cards charge up to 45% a year, and 72 ÷ 45 is under two years.

example.ask: Tap why the debt doubles.
parts: Arav owes ₹5,000 on a card at 36% a year,
and he leaves it unpaid,
so in about two years he owes near ₹10,000.
example.spot: and he leaves it unpaid,
example.feedback: An unpaid balance keeps gathering interest, so 36% doubles it in about two years.

guided.stem: A loan app charges 24% a year on an unpaid sum. Roughly how fast does it double?
guided.hint: Share 72 out by the yearly charge.

options.feedback: Yes. 72 ÷ 24 is 3, so the sum doubles in about three years.
That uses the rate as the time. 72 ÷ 24 gives about three years.
That would be a 6% rate. At 24% it doubles in about three.

guided.stem: Which grows faster: savings at 6% or a debt at 18%?
guided.hint: Work out the doubling time for each one.

options.feedback: Right. It doubles in about 4 years; the savings take about 12.
Savings at 6% take about 12 years to double. The debt takes about 4.
A higher rate doubles faster, so the 18% debt grows about three times as fast.

steps.takeaway: High-interest debt doubles fast; at 36% it takes about two years.

steps.title: Only for a steady rate

hook.stem: A fund gained 20% last year and fell 5% this year. What does 72 ÷ 20 tell you about it?

options.text: Not much, as the rate did not stay steady.
options.feedback: Right. The rule needs one rate that holds. This fund's return jumped around.
That would need 20% every year. Last year's gain is no promise.
72 is only the number you divide. The real issue is that the rate changes.

steps.teach: For shares, the rule can only say: if it grew 12% every year, it would double in 6. Real years go up and down, so no single rate fits.

example.ask: Tap the part that breaks the shortcut.
parts: Jaya's fund rose 15% one year,
then dropped 10% the next,
so 72 ÷ 15 cannot give its doubling time.
example.spot: then dropped 10% the next,
example.feedback: The return changed from year to year, so no single rate fits the rule.

guided.stem: Which case suits the rule of 72 best?
guided.hint: Look for a number that holds still.

options.feedback: Yes. A fixed rate is just what the rule needs.

options.text: A share that rose 30% last year.
options.feedback: One good year does not set future returns, so the rule is only a what-if here.

options.text: A fund whose return changes monthly.
options.feedback: A return that keeps changing gives the rule no steady rate.

guided.stem: A friend says 72 ÷ 12 proves his share will double in six years. What is the flaw?
guided.hint: Ask whether next year must match this one.

options.feedback: Right. The sum is fine, but a share has no steady 12% to rely on.

options.text: The sum is off; it gives eight years.
options.feedback: The sum is right: 72 ÷ 12 is 6. The flaw is treating the rate as fixed.

options.text: He is right; one good year sets the rate.
options.feedback: One good year does not set the next. The rule only guesses for steady rates.

steps.takeaway: The rule needs a steady rate; markets do not give one.

concepts.title: Risk and return
concepts.hook: A sure ₹12, or a coin flip for ₹30 or nothing. The flip could pay more, or nothing. The range of results matters.
concepts.rule: A bigger possible gain often comes with more chance of loss or a wider range of results. A high possible return is not a sure return.

claims.text: Investment risk includes the chance of loss and uncertain results.
A high possible gain may mean more risk. The gain is not sure.

Cash savings are the safest of the three main kinds of assets but earn the least; shares carry the most risk and have earned the most over time. A bond is a loan to a company, and investors want higher returns for taking more risk.
In the US, large company shares as a group have dropped in value in about one year out of every three.
A longer time to a goal gives more room to wait out ups and downs; money needed soon usually suits lower-risk places.

items.stem: Your shares came back at ₹2,700, a 10% loss on what you put in. About what did you put in?

options.feedback: Yes. A 10% loss leaves nine tenths, and nine tenths of ₹3,000 is ₹2,700.
The 10% was taken from the start, not from ₹2,700. Divide ₹2,700 by 0.9 to get ₹3,000.
That takes another 10% off. Going back to the start means undoing the loss, which gives ₹3,000.

items.stem: Om says shares of a big, famous company cannot go down. What is wrong?

options.feedback: Right. Any share price can fall, and even large companies' shares as a group have had many losing years.

options.text: They can drop, but bounce back within a week.
options.feedback: Nothing sets how fast a price recovers. A drop can last a long time, or not recover.

options.text: He is right; famous names hold their price.
options.feedback: Fame does not hold a price up. Large-company shares can and do fall in value.

items.stem: Two summer jobs: one pays a sure ₹6,000. The other pays sales commission, anywhere from ₹0 to ₹15,000. Which one carries risk?

options.feedback: Yes. Its result is unsure and could be zero. That chance of getting less than hoped is risk.

options.text: The fixed-pay job, since it cannot pay more.
options.feedback: Missing out on a bigger amount is not the risk here. The fixed job's result is known in advance.

options.text: Neither, since both are honest work.
options.feedback: Risk is not about honesty. It is about how unsure the result is, and only one pay is unsure.

items.stem: A college friend's crypto app is up 40% this month. What does that tell you about next month?

options.text: Nothing sure; big jumps can reverse just as fast.
options.feedback: Right. Things that rise sharply also swing sharply, so a big gain is no promise of the next one.
One month sets no pattern. Bigger possible gains come with bigger possible falls.

options.text: It has become a low-risk choice.
options.feedback: A sharp rise shows big swings, which is the mark of more risk, not less.

items.stem: Cash is the safest of the three main kinds. What risk does it still carry?

options.text: Rising prices can shrink what it buys.
options.feedback: Yes. Cash rarely loses rupees, but if prices rise faster than it earns, it buys less.

options.text: None, since its rupee value holds still.
options.feedback: The rupee amount holds, but rising prices can still cut what it buys over time.
Cash swings far less than shares. Its main worry is prices rising faster than it earns.

items.stem: A fund paid a very high return last year. What does that suggest about how it behaves?

options.text: It probably swings a lot, up and down.
options.feedback: Right. High returns usually come with bigger swings, so a big gain hints at big possible falls.

options.text: It is low-risk, since it clearly works.
options.feedback: A big gain does not show safety. Riskier things are the ones that can pay more, and lose more.

options.text: It will pay the same high return every year.
options.feedback: One year sets no promise. A high-return fund can also have bad years.

items.stem: You need ₹20,000 in 6 months, and ₹2 lakh in 28 years. Where does each fit?

options.text: Savings for the first; more swing suits the second.
options.feedback: Yes. Money needed soon has no time to recover, while a far goal can ride out dips.

options.text: Shares for both, to earn the most.
options.feedback: Shares could drop just before the 6-month goal, with no time to recover.

options.text: Savings for both, since shares can fall at the worst time.
options.feedback: Shares can fall, but 28 years gives time to wait out dips, so the far goal can take more swing.

items.stem: Tara saves for a goal 40 years away, but she needs ₹50,000 of it in two years for a course. Where does that part fit?

options.text: In low-risk savings, since that part is needed soon.
options.feedback: Right. The long goal does not help money you need in two years, so that part needs a safe place.

options.text: In shares, like the rest, since her goal is far off.
options.feedback: Only the far-off part has time to wait out dips. The course money is due soon.

options.text: In one fast-rising share, to grow it quickly.
options.feedback: One share swings the most, and a drop could hit just when the course fee is due.

steps.title: Risk means you could get back less

hook.stem: You put ₹1,000 into one company's shares. What could it be worth in a year?

options.feedback: Right. Share prices move, so you could end up above or below what you paid.
Nothing holds a share price up. It can end below what you paid.
A gain is possible, not promised. The price can fall too.

steps.teach: Risk is the chance that the result is not what you hoped. Prices of shares and funds move, so you could get back less than you put in, or even nothing.

nodes: Get back more, less or nothing

example.ask: Tap the risk.
parts: Sahil buys ₹2,000 of one company's shares,
hoping for a gain by Diwali,
but its price could drop below what he paid.
example.spot: but its price could drop below what he paid.
example.feedback: Risk is the chance of ending up with less than you put in.

guided.stem: Which of these has the least risk of giving back less than you put in?
guided.hint: Look for the one whose value holds still.

options.text: Cash in a bank savings account.
options.feedback: Yes. Cash savings are the safest of the main choices.
A single share can drop a lot, so it carries more risk.

options.text: A share a friend says will double.
options.feedback: A tip is not a promise. That share can still fall.

guided.stem: A share's price swings a lot from week to week. What does that tell you?
guided.hint: Ask how easy the end point is to know.

options.feedback: Right. Wide swings mean you cannot be sure where it ends.
Swings go both ways. Big swings can end in a loss too.

options.text: It cannot fall below what you paid.
options.feedback: Nothing stops a price falling below your cost.

steps.takeaway: Risk is the chance of getting back less than you put in.

steps.title: Bigger possible return, bigger swings

hook.stem: Which has usually earned the most over many years: cash savings, bonds or shares?

options.feedback: Right. Shares have earned the most over time, but they also swing the most.
Cash is the safest, but it has earned the least of the three.
Bonds sit in the middle, with less swing than shares and smaller returns.

steps.teach: A bond is a loan you make to a company. Shares swing most and have earned most; cash is safest and earns least; bonds sit between. People want more reward for bigger swings, so riskier things tend to pay more.

visual.label: Risk and return of three kinds

example.ask: Tap the price of the higher return.
parts: Shares have earned more than cash over long spans,
but they swing much more along the way,
so the extra return comes with extra risk.
example.spot: but they swing much more along the way,
example.feedback: The extra return is paid for with bigger ups and downs.

guided.stem: A scheme promises share-like returns with no risk at all. What does that tell you?
guided.hint: Recall what pays for any extra gain.

options.text: The claim does not fit how risk works.
options.feedback: Yes. A high return with no risk is a warning sign.

options.text: It is a rare safe bargain.
options.feedback: Higher returns come with more risk. A no-risk promise does not add up.
Shares still swing. The promise is what is wrong.

guided.stem: Bonds usually swing less than shares. What do they usually give up?
guided.hint: Recall what a calmer ride costs.

options.feedback: Right. Less swing usually comes with more modest returns.
Bonds are usually safer than shares, not less safe.
The calmer ride usually costs some return.

steps.takeaway: A chance of more gain comes with bigger ups and downs.

steps.title: Time decides how much swing you can wait out

hook.stem: Money for next month's college fee: where does it fit best?

options.feedback: Right. Money needed soon has no time to recover from a drop.
Shares could drop just before the fee is due, with no time to recover.

options.text: A fund that rose fast last year.
options.feedback: A fast riser can fall fast too, and the fee is due very soon.

steps.teach: If you need money soon, a drop could hit just when you need it, so short-term money suits low-risk savings. A far-off goal gives time to wait out the dips.

left.title: Goal next month
lines: No time to wait out a dip

example.ask: Tap why she keeps it in savings.
parts: Aditi needs ₹30,000 for exam fees in March,
so she keeps it in a savings account,
because a fall in shares could hit just then.
example.spot: because a fall in shares could hit just then.
example.feedback: Money needed soon has no time to recover from a drop.

guided.stem: Share prices fall in some years. Who is hurt most by such a drop?
guided.hint: Ask who has no time to wait for a recovery.

options.text: Someone who needs the money next month.
options.feedback: Yes. They may have to sell at the low price.

options.text: Someone saving for 25 years from now.
options.feedback: They have years to wait for prices to recover.

options.text: No one, since prices bounce back next day.
options.feedback: Recoveries can take a long time, not one day.

guided.stem: Raj, 22, saves for a goal 30 years away. What does the long wait give him?
guided.hint: Think about what thirty years allows after a bad year.

options.text: Time to ride out ups and downs.
options.feedback: Right. A long horizon gives room to wait out bad years.
Time helps, but losses are still possible.

options.text: No reason to think about risk.
options.feedback: Risk still matters; he just has more time to handle it.

steps.takeaway: Money needed soon belongs where drops are unlikely.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.hook: A monsoon cancels cricket practice and hurts both a bat seller and a ball seller. Two products can still share one shock.
concepts.rule: Spreading money across many firms and industries can cut the harm from one weak part. It cannot make all loss go away, since many parts can fall together.

claims.text: A mix of holdings can spread the risk from one firm.
A broad mix can cut some risk from one firm. It cannot promise you will not lose if the whole market drops.
Four or five shares are not a real spread. One investor guide asks for at least a dozen, across many industries.
A fund that holds just one industry does not give a full spread on its own.
Each extra holding can add fees, and fees lower your returns.

items.stem: One of your equal holdings went to zero, and your whole mix fell about 5%. About how many holdings do you have?

options.feedback: Each holding is one part of the whole. If one part is 5%, there are 100 ÷ 5 = 20 parts.
Five is the percent that fell, not the count. One part worth 5% means 20 equal parts.

options.text: About 95, the share that was left.
options.feedback: The 95% left is a percent, not a count. One holding worth 5% means 20 holdings in all.

items.stem: At the college canteen, Tanvi's stall sells only cold drinks, while Rohan sells cold drinks, tea and snacks. A cold week cuts cold-drink sales. Whose sales hold up better?

options.text: Rohan's, since tea and snacks still sell.
options.feedback: His other goods keep earning while cold drinks slow down, so one weak line hurts less.

options.text: Tanvi's, since she knows one drink well.
options.feedback: Knowing one drink well does not help when buyers stop wanting it. She has nothing else to sell.

options.text: Both drop by the same amount.
options.feedback: Only Tanvi depends on cold drinks alone. Rohan has other things buyers still want.

items.stem: Splitting ₹8,000 as ₹7,000 in one firm and ₹1,000 in another barely helps, because ___.

options.text: most of the money still rides on one firm
options.feedback: Yes. If the big holding has a bad year, most of your money takes the hit anyway.

options.text: two firms are worse than one
options.feedback: Two firms are not worse. The problem is the uneven split, with most money in one place.

options.text: the small holding is sure to fall
options.feedback: Nothing says the small one will fall. The weak point is that one firm holds most of the money.

items.stem: Your friend's mix fell sharply in a year when only IT firms did badly. What does that tell you about the mix?

options.text: Much of it was in IT firms.
options.feedback: Right. A slump in one industry can only hit hard if a big part of the money sits there.
More industries would soften an IT slump, not deepen it. The sharp fall points to too much in IT.

options.text: It was hit by a fall across the whole market.
options.feedback: Only IT did badly that year, so the drop came from holding a lot in that one industry.

items.stem: Aman says adding more and more funds always makes his mix better. What is he missing?

options.text: Each extra fund adds fees that cut returns.
options.feedback: Right. More holdings usually bring more fees and costs, which lower what you keep.
A wider mix can lower risk. The catch is the extra fees each one adds.

options.text: He is right; each fund adds safety.
options.feedback: Spreading helps up to a point, but each extra fund also adds costs that eat into returns.

items.stem: Match each mix to what it really gives you.

options.feedback: Different industries help, but five holdings are still too few to spread well.
This fits a mix with a good variety but not enough holdings, like five firms.
Twelve names in one industry still move together when banking has a bad year.
This is what you carry when every holding sits in the same kind of business.

options.text: A dozen firms across eight industries
options.feedback: Enough holdings in different industries make the spread real, so one slump cannot hit them all.
This fits a mix with enough firms and enough variety between them.

items.stem: Your college fest has stalls run by twelve different clubs. A cyclone warning cancels the whole fest. What happens to the stalls' sales?

options.text: Nearly all of them drop together.
options.feedback: Right. Many stalls protect against one stall's bad day, not a shock that shuts the whole fest.

options.text: Twelve clubs keep total sales steady.
options.feedback: Many stalls help only when trouble hits one of them. A cancelled fest hits every stall.

options.text: The food stalls lose sales, the rest do fine.
options.feedback: The warning cancels everything, so every kind of stall loses its buyers at once.

items.stem: What does a spread over many firms still leave you open to?

options.text: Falls that hit almost all firms at once.
options.feedback: A spread softens one firm's trouble, but a market-wide fall pulls most holdings down together.

options.text: No risk, once you hold enough firms.
options.feedback: No number of firms stops a fall that hits the whole market at the same time.

options.text: The bad luck of one single firm.
options.feedback: One firm's bad luck is what a spread does guard against. The open risk is a fall across the market.

misconceptions.name: One basket is enough
misconceptions.correction: One firm or sector leaves a lot tied to one outcome.

misconceptions.name: Many means no loss
misconceptions.correction: Many holdings can still fall at the same time.

misconceptions.name: Many names means a spread
misconceptions.correction: Many firms in one industry still share the same risk.

misconceptions.name: More funds is always better
misconceptions.correction: Each extra holding can add fees, which lower returns.

steps.title: Spread money so one loss is not everything

hook.stem: All your savings sit in one company's shares, and it has a terrible year. What happens to your savings?

options.feedback: Right. With every rupee in one firm, its bad year becomes your bad year.

options.text: They stay safe, since shares bounce back.
options.feedback: Shares can fall and stay down. With one firm, nothing else is there to soften the drop.

options.text: Only a small part of them falls.
options.feedback: That only happens with a spread. Here all the money sits in the one firm that fell.

steps.teach: Diversification means you do not keep all your money in one place, so if one holding does badly, the rest can make up for part of it.

left.title: All in one firm
lines: One bad year hits it all

right.title: Spread over ten firms
lines: One bad year hits a tenth

example.ask: Tap the part that softens the blow.
parts: Farhan splits his savings over eight firms,
and when one firm has a bad year,
the other seven keep most of his money steady.
example.spot: the other seven keep most of his money steady.
example.feedback: The healthy holdings carry on, so one weak firm hurts only a small slice.

guided.stem: Meera puts ₹10,000 into one firm. Om splits ₹10,000 over five firms. One firm in each mix halves. Who has more left?
guided.hint: Work out how much of each person's money sat in the weak firm.

options.feedback: Yes. Om loses half of ₹2,000, so ₹1,000. Meera loses half of all ₹10,000.

options.text: Meera, since one firm is easier to watch.

guided.stem: Which mix spreads the risk from one company the most?

options.feedback: Right. Ten firms means one bad firm touches only a tenth of the money.
All the money rides on one firm, so there is no spread at all.
Two firms is a small spread. One bad firm would still hit half the money.

steps.takeaway: Spread money over many holdings so one bad firm hurts less.

steps.title: A real spread needs many firms in many industries

hook.stem: You own shares in twelve firms, and all of them are banks. Are you spread out?

options.text: Not really; one bad year for banks hits all twelve.
options.feedback: Right. Firms in one industry rise and fall together, so twelve banks act almost like one bet.
The count looks fine, but every firm shares the same business, so one slump reaches them all.

options.text: Yes, as long as they are big banks.
options.feedback: Size does not change the shared risk. A bad year for banking hits big and small banks alike.

steps.teach: Firms in one industry rise and fall together, so a cement slump hits every cement firm. A real spread needs a dozen or more firms in different industries, though each extra holding can add fees.

example.ask: Tap the hidden risk.
parts: Kabir owns twelve shares,
but all twelve are cement firms,
so one slump in building hits them all.
example.spot: but all twelve are cement firms,
example.feedback: Twelve names in one industry still share one fate. A spread needs different industries too.

guided.stem: Sana holds five tech shares. Riya holds twelve shares in banks, food, power and medicine. Whose mix is closer to a real spread?
guided.hint: Look at both how many firms and how different they are.

options.feedback: Yes. She has a dozen firms spread across several industries, which is a real spread.
Fast growth is not a spread. Five firms in one industry can all fall together.

options.text: Both are the same, since both hold shares.
options.feedback: Holding shares is not enough. How many firms and how many industries matter.

guided.stem: A fund holds only medicine companies. Does owning it give you a full spread?
guided.hint: Check how many industries sit inside the fund.

options.text: No, it sits in one industry.
options.feedback: Right. A fund focused on one industry does not give a full spread on its own.

options.text: Yes, any fund is spread out.
options.feedback: A fund can still bet on one industry. Then one bad patch hits the whole fund.

options.text: Yes, if it holds over fifty firms.
options.feedback: Fifty firms in one industry still share one fate. The industries need to differ too.

steps.takeaway: A real spread means many firms across many different industries.

steps.title: A mix cuts risk but cannot remove it

hook.stem: You hold shares in thirty firms, and the whole market falls hard one month. What happens?

options.text: Most of your holdings fall together.
options.feedback: Right. A fall across the whole market pulls nearly every firm down at once.

options.text: Thirty firms keep you fully safe.
options.feedback: A spread guards against one firm's trouble, not a fall that hits almost every firm.

options.text: Only one or two of them fall.
options.feedback: When the whole market drops, most firms drop with it, not just a couple.

steps.teach: A spread guards against one firm's bad luck, because the others carry on. It cannot stop a shock that hits nearly all firms at once, like a big market fall.

example.ask: Tap the shock a spread cannot stop.
parts: Neel's twenty shares cover many industries,
yet a sharp fall across the whole market
pulls almost all of them down together.
example.spot: yet a sharp fall across the whole market
example.feedback: A fall across the whole market hits nearly every holding, so a spread only softens it.

guided.stem: Which trouble can a wide spread protect you from best?
guided.hint: Ask how much of the mix the trouble touches.

options.text: A fire at one firm's factory.
options.feedback: Yes. Only one holding is hurt, so the rest of the mix carries on.

options.text: A crash across the whole market.

concepts.title: Index funds and stock picking
concepts.hook: An index fund holds a whole basket of companies. One chosen stock rides on a single company.
concepts.rule: An index fund copies an index's firms in the same mix, with low fees. It rises and falls with that index, a little behind after costs.

claims.text: An index fund holds securities to follow a named index and charges an expense ratio.
Over ten years, most active large-cap funds in India did worse than their index. The share varies by year and fund group.
An index fund holds all or most of the shares in its index, in the same proportions, instead of relying on a manager to pick.
Index funds follow a passive plan with little trading, so their expense ratios are lower than active funds.
Tracking error is the small gap between an index fund and its index, caused by expenses and running costs.

concepts.title: UPI scams and social engineering
concepts.hook: A fake prize message may ask for a UPI PIN to make a payment look like a receipt.
concepts.rule: A scam story can steer a person to approve a payment. A UPI PIN approves payments; receiving never needs it. No one else needs your PIN or OTP. If tricked, tell your bank and call 1930.

claims.text: NPCI warns that a QR scan and UPI PIN can be used to make a payment, not collect a prize.

Since 1 October 2025, people can no longer send each other UPI collect requests; merchants still can, for genuine business use. Scam messages also use links or QR codes that promise rewards for your PIN.
RBI says getting money never needs a QR scan or a PIN, so take care if asked for either.
RBI says never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone, not even bank staff, and not to download unknown apps on your phone.
RBI says to tell your bank at once about a debit you did not make, and block debits, including UPI. Money taken by fraud can be reported on the 1930 helpline or cybercrime.gov.in.

items.stem: A message with a bank logo says 'Enter your UPI PIN to receive your refund.' Why is it a trick, however real it looks?

options.text: A PIN only sends money, so it would pay out, not in.
options.feedback: Right. Receiving needs no PIN, so a request for one to get paid is a payment in disguise.

options.text: Refunds come by cheque, not UPI.
options.feedback: Refunds can come by UPI. The point is that getting money never needs your PIN.

options.text: Real banks do not put their logos on refund messages.
options.feedback: Real banks use logos too. A neat logo can still sit on a false story.

items.stem: Match each UPI moment to what it means for your money.

options.feedback: Your PIN is your approval, so money leaves your account.
Money only leaves when you approve a payment with your PIN.
When a friend sends you money, you do nothing but receive it.
Getting money needs no PIN and no scan from you.
A QR scan sets up a payment from you to whoever made the code.
This is what a scan does: it opens a payment from your account.

items.stem: You buy groceries and scan the shop's UPI QR code to pay the bill. Is entering your PIN right here?

options.text: Yes; you mean to pay, so the PIN approves your own payment.
options.feedback: Right. The PIN is meant for paying. The trick is only when someone says it will bring money in.

options.text: No; a PIN should not be typed on a QR payment.
options.feedback: You do need your PIN to pay. Just never enter it to receive money or share it.

options.text: Only if the shop sends you money first.
options.feedback: Paying a shop needs no money from them. Your PIN simply approves your payment.

items.stem: Three links each ask for your UPI PIN to claim ₹1,500 'cashback'. If you enter your PIN on all three, about how much leaves you?

options.feedback: Each PIN entry approves a ₹1,500 payment. Three times ₹1,500 is ₹4,500 out of your account.
A PIN never brings money in. Each entry sends ₹1,500 out.
The cashback label is the bait. Each PIN entry is a real payment of ₹1,500.

items.stem: A caller who gets your OTP can move your money, because the OTP ___.

options.text: approves payments as if it were you
options.feedback: Yes. The OTP is a key for approving a payment, so whoever has it can act as you.
An OTP is not a name check. It approves a payment or login, which is why it stays secret.
It lasts long enough to be used, which is why a scammer asks for it at once.

items.stem: Sam says real bank staff are allowed to ask for his UPI PIN. What is wrong?

options.text: No one needs his PIN, not even real bank staff.
options.feedback: Right. A PIN is never shared, with anyone, however genuine the caller sounds.

options.text: Bank staff may ask, but just on weekdays.
options.feedback: The day does not matter. No one at a bank ever needs his PIN.

options.text: He is right; staff need it to fix accounts.
options.feedback: Banks can fix accounts without his PIN. Anyone asking for it is a warning sign.

options.text: Tell your bank, block UPI, then report it.

options.text: Wait for the caller to send it back.

options.text: Keep quiet, since you shared the OTP yourself.
options.feedback: Being tricked is common and not shameful. Reporting fast is what helps.

options.text: No; reports are just for money taken.
options.feedback: Suspected fraud messages can be reported too, through Chakshu on Sanchar Saathi.

options.text: Reply to the text to warn the sender off.
options.feedback: Replying only keeps you in touch with the scammer. Report the text on Chakshu instead.
